title: The young teacher under the banyan
hookLine: old sages sit before a young, silent teacher under a banyan, and Yoga names the teacher of the first teachers
carry: ishvara: the teacher of the first teachers
tomorrow: a king gives up his throne, then can't stop thinking about a fawn. where does it lead?

cards: Under a great banyan tree, the old story goes, four sages sit. They are old and white-haired, wise already, and they still carry doubts they can't untie. Facing them sits their teacher, and he's young.
Barely more than a boy. He doesn't say a word. And one by one, as they sit in his silence, their doubts fall away.
An old verse, still chanted, calls it a wonder: the students are old, the teacher is young, and the teaching is silence. The teacher is Shiva, as Dakshinamurti, the one who faces south.

teach.b: Dakshinamurti is honored as the first teacher, and you can find him on the south-facing wall of many Shiva temples, especially in South India, sitting under his tree.
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras make the same move in philosophy. Stillness can come, he says, through devotion to Ishvara, the Lord.
And Ishvara is a particular purusha, a witness never touched by the afflictions, by actions or by their ripening. Then the line that answers the banyan.
Ishvara is the teacher of even the earliest teachers, because time doesn't limit him. Every teacher had a teacher. At the top of the line, Yoga places one who never had to be a beginner.

teach.h: YOGA ADDS A LORD TO THE MAP.
teach.b: This is where Yoga parts from Samkhya: Samkhya's count, as we heard it, left no place for a Lord, and Yoga keeps the same map and sets Ishvara above it. Then Patanjali gives the way to reach him: his word is Om.
Repeat it, and dwell on its meaning. This isn't only theory. It's a living Hindu habit.

teach.h: OM, AND THE LINE OF TEACHERS.
teach.b: Before a lesson in the Veda, in music or in dance, many teachers chant Om and bow to the guru parampara, the line of teachers, often in a verse that begins with Shiva or Narayana and ends with my own teacher.
Students touch the teacher's feet. One full moon each year, Guru Purnima, is kept for honoring teachers. You're never learning from just one person.
You're joining a line that, for the tradition, starts with the Lord.

how: Many Hindu students begin a lesson in scripture, music or dance by chanting Om and bowing to the guru parampara, the line of teachers, and Guru Purnima is kept each year to honor teachers; in the Yoga Sutras, devotion to Ishvara, the teacher of even the earliest teachers, is one way toward stillness.

games.q: before your first lesson, your music teacher chants om and names her own teachers. in Yoga's terms, where does that line end?
o: with Ishvara, the teacher of the earliest teachers
nowhere: each teacher just invents it
games.why: Ishvara. Patanjali calls him the teacher of even the earliest teachers, and his word is Om, the sound your lesson started with.

practice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that stuck, then the person who taught them, if you know, and let the line run back as far as it goes. Bow your head a little to the whole line.
If you pray, say Om softly a few times, as the sutras describe, and dwell on its meaning. If you don't, say thank you once for each teacher you can name.

wordCard.voice: Yoga. The school that keeps Samkhya's map and adds Ishvara, the teacher of even the earliest teachers, whose word is Om.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the Lord; in the Yoga Sutras, a particular purusha untouched by afflictions and actions.

carryVoice: Your line: Ishvara, the teacher of the first teachers. Every line of teachers has a top, and Yoga names who sits there. Rest well.
